To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

acute mental stress increases brain activity in the prefrontal cortex and posterior pariet cortex specifically during the maintenance phase of working memory, whereas hippocampal activity is modulated by acute stress during encoding and/or retrieval.

acute psychosocial mental stress increased WM accuracy and activity in the prefrontal cortex and parietal cortex specifically during maintenance of WM, whereas stress decreased hippocampal activity during encoding and retrieval.

acute stress increases brain activity in prefrontal cortex and posterior parietals during maintenance of items within working memory, while stress decreases activity in hippocampus during retrieval of items.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of acute stress exposure on the brain activity underlying WM.
the question of how stress affects the brain during memory processes.
the effects of acute stress in healthy humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
acute psychosocial mental stress increases WM performance and modulates WM-related brain activity in the PFC and hippocampus.
stress affects WM performance in men and that this effect is associated with a stress-induced modulation of brain activity in the PFC, PPC, and hippocampus.
stress increases activity of the prefrontal cortex and parietal cortex, while it decreases activity in the hippocampal region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
acute psychosocial mental stress in humans increases activity in brain regions involved in WM maintenance and decreases activity in brain regions that are involved in WM encoding and retrieval.
acute stress increases PFC and PPC activity during WM maintenance, whereas hippocampal activity is modulated by stress at different phases of WM processing.
acute stress can modulate brain activity in the PFC and PPC during maintenance of WM, whereas effects of stress on the hippocampus are restricted to encoding or retrieval.
The main takeaway from our work is that
acute stress can have both positive and negative effects on WM performance and neural activity.
stress affects WM-related brain activity in a task-dependent manner.
the effects of acute stress are not limited to specific cognitive domains but rather affect a wide variety of cognitive processes.
